record.paper_title: Monetary Stabilization in Cryptocurrencies—Design Approaches and Open Questions
record.original_question: Can a stablecoin obtain secure permissionless oracle data for its chosen nominal anchor, such as exchange-rate or price information needed for monetary policy, without reinstating a globally trusted party or trusted group?

evidence.quote:
Even then, however, a fully permissionless mode of operation
is only possible under a signiﬁcant caveat—the existence
of a secure (permissionless) oracle for the chosen nominal
anchor. Oracles are system components that transfer ”external”
information onto the blockchain. Monetary information, such
as the price of the cryptocurrency relative to another currency,
are required for monetary policy mechanisms. They are typ-
ically not natively generated ”on-chain” and must therefore
be provided by an oracle. Oracles can be trivially realized
using a trusted party that vouches for the correctness of
data by means of cryptographic signatures. However, this
clearly reinstates a globally trusted actor (or a group thereof).
Completely permissionless oracles are, on the other hand, still
an active research ﬁeld, with no sufﬁciently secure solutions
for, e.g., transferring price data, currently in sight [4].

We identify a number of further opportunities for technical
and economics research on cryptocurrency stabilization, such
as on the resilience of self-tokenizing techniques, on the
viability of secure permissionless price feeds for informing
policing decisions, and on the actual effectiveness of monetary
policy given the complete transparency of both the policy and
its enforcement.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a cryptocurrency protocol operating on a permissionless distributed ledger that aims to maintain a stable nominal value relative to a chosen external anchor (for example, a fiat currency or a basket of goods). Implementing a monetary policy that targets such an anchor requires the protocol to have access, on-chain, to external information such as the current exchange rate or price of the cryptocurrency relative to the anchor. A component that supplies such external information to the ledger is called an oracle. An oracle is said to be permissionless if its operation does not rely on any fixed, globally trusted party or fixed group of trusted parties (whether identified by signing keys, identities, or otherwise) whose honesty must be assumed for the correctness of the reported data; instead, any party should be able to participate in or verify the data-supply process under the protocol's open-membership rules.

Question: Does there exist a mechanism by which a stablecoin protocol on a permissionless ledger can obtain external price or exchange-rate information for its nominal anchor, with provable security guarantees against manipulation, without reintroducing a globally trusted party or trusted committee whose honesty must be assumed? Equivalently, is it possible to design a secure permissionless price-feed oracle suitable for informing on-chain monetary policy decisions, and if so, characterize the assumptions (economic, cryptographic, or game-theoretic) under which such security can be established; if not, prove an impossibility result delineating the obstruction.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem of designing secure permissionless price-feed oracles for stablecoins remains an active research area. Existing systems (Chainlink, Witnet, Tellor, DIA, UMA) provide decentralized oracle networks using staking, reputation, aggregation of node reports, or optimistic dispute mechanisms, but each still relies on assumptions about a sufficiently honest set of participants, economic incentives, or fallback governance, and price-oracle manipulations remain a documented attack surface in DeFi. No solution has been established as fully secure under purely permissionless assumptions without some trusted-set or economic-honesty assumption, so the question as posed appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Smart Contract Security Guidelines #3: The Dangers of Price Oracles
status_evidence.snippet: Discussion of ongoing vulnerabilities and manipulation risks in price oracles used by DeFi and stablecoin systems.
status_evidence.claim: Price oracle manipulation remains a major and unresolved security concern for on-chain financial protocols.

status_evidence.title: AiRacleX: Automated Detection of Price Oracle Manipulations
status_evidence.snippet: Recent (2025) research devoted to detecting price oracle manipulations indicates the problem of secure price feeds is still actively studied.
status_evidence.claim: Secure permissionless price oracles remain an active research topic with continuing manipulation incidents.

status_evidence.title: The Next Step for Stablecoins: Decentralized Oracles
status_evidence.snippet: Trusted feed models are vulnerable to centralization and collusion attacks; decentralized permissionless alternatives such as Witnet are still being developed.
status_evidence.claim: Trusted-party oracles are recognized as inadequate, and fully permissionless secure alternatives are still under development.
